title: King & Pawn Endgames
description: Six drills on fresh random positions every time. Nothing interrupts you while you play: if a move throws the result away, the game runs to its real finish and the post-mortem shows you which move did it.
source: Principles from GothamChess, "EASY CHESS ENDGAMES: King & Pawns". King and pawn against king is solved inside the page and works offline; the pawn race is looked up in Lichess's endgame tablebase, so that drill needs a connection.

drills.name: Catch the runaway pawn
drills.goal: A pawn is running and their king is too far away to help. Catch it.
drills.idea: The rule of the square: count the squares from the pawn to its queening square, and picture a box of that size stretching across toward your king. If your king is inside that box, or can step into it, the pawn is caught. Moving straight at the queening square keeps you inside the box.

drills.name: Escort the pawn home
drills.goal: You are a pawn up with a won position. Queen it.
drills.idea: Your king is the escort and goes first. Take the opposition so their king has to give way, outflank diagonally when it steps aside, and push the pawn only while it stays behind your king or once the path is clear.

drills.name: Hold the draw a pawn down
drills.goal: You are a pawn down but the position is drawn. Stop the pawn.
drills.idea: Three moves hold almost every one of these: stand in front of the pawn whenever that square is free, retreat straight back on the pawn's own file when it advances, and face their king to take the opposition when it comes up the side.

drills.name: The rook pawn draw
drills.goal: They have an a- or h-pawn. Hold the corner.
drills.idea: A rook pawn can never be escorted home. There is no file on the far side to outflank you on, so the corner is a fortress: reach it and shuffle there, and any attempt to force you out is stalemate.

drills.name: Win the pawn race
drills.goal: A pawn each and both are running. Queen first, or stop theirs.
drills.idea: Count both races before you touch anything. Then use the king for two jobs at once: shoulder their king onto the long way round, and escort your own pawn. Do not stop to grab their pawn if the capture lets their king back into the game.

drills.name: Random position
drills.goal: One of the drills above, and you are not told which. Work out what the position is worth, then go and get it.
drills.idea: Read the position before you move: whose pawn is it, is it a rook pawn, is the defending king inside the square, and who holds the opposition. The technique follows from the answer.

principles.title: The rule of the square
principles.text: Count the squares from the pawn to its queening square and extend a box of that size toward the defending king. A king inside the box, or able to step into it, catches the pawn. Build the box from the square in front of a pawn still on its starting rank, so the double step is accounted for.

principles.title: The opposition
principles.text: Kings face each other on the same file or rank with one square between. Whoever does not have to move holds it, and the other king has to give way. The gaps that matter are odd, so both coordinate differences come out even.

principles.title: Outflanking
principles.text: Holding the opposition, when their king steps to one side, step diagonally forward to the other. That takes the squares in front of your pawn.

principles.title: The king is the escort
principles.text: Keep the king in front of the pawn and move it first. Push the pawn only while it stays behind the king, to hand the move back to them, or when their king has stepped beside the pawn instead of in front of it and the path is clear.

principles.title: Defending: file discipline
principles.text: Step directly in front of the pawn whenever that square is free, retreat straight back along the pawn's file when it advances, and step in front of their king to take the opposition when it comes up the side. On the back rank this becomes stalemate and the draw holds.

principles.title: The rook pawn exception
principles.text: An a- or h-pawn is drawn whenever the defending king reaches the corner, because the edge of the board removes the files needed to outflank. An attacking king that gets stuck in front of its own rook pawn can even be stalemated there.

principles.title: Distant opposition and waiting moves
principles.text: Opposition works at three and five squares too. When stepping straight forward would let them take the direct opposition, step wider instead and make them commit first; the extra tempo flips the opposition your way.

principles.title: Shouldering in a race
principles.text: In a race, do not run straight at the target. Step so your king stands beside theirs and forces it onto a wider arc; every tempo it loses is one your pawn gains. For the same reason, do not stop to capture a pawn when the capture opens a path for their king.

principles.title: Breakthroughs and centralisation
principles.text: Before racing, check whether a pawn lever gives them a passed pawn outside your king's square. Prefer the centralising move that does two jobs at once, and spend a pawn move to kill the breakthrough when one exists.
